subtitulo: A country made of refugees administering Europe's outer border (2015 – 2026)

coda.heading: Resonances 2024–2026 and coda for the trip
intro: In 2026, the Aegean route remains active at lower volumes than in 2015 but steadily so, and others have grown: the Libyan route to Crete and the Peloponnese, which in 2025 led the Greek government to temporarily suspend the processing of asylum claims for arrivals from North Africa, a measure condemned by human-rights bodies and by the Commission itself. And the whole of southern Europe is debating the same thing: containment, externalization, agreements with third countries.

items.text: For your trip, two local observations. The first: Corfu sits a few kilometers from Albania, the Union's outer border, with regular traffic of people and goods, and a large, established Albanian community that has been in Greece since the 1990s — the country's largest migrant minority, with a history of intense stigmatization in that decade and of considerable integration since. If you talk with someone of Albanian origin, you'll find a two-generation trajectory that illustrates how a migrant group's place changes once another arrives behind it.

closing: The second: the port of Igoumenitsa, across from Corfu, is the departure point for ferries to Italy and therefore a transit point toward northern Europe, with the truck-control practices that entails. The Ionian corridor from entrega 1 — the hinge between the eastern and western Mediterranean — remains exactly that, now operating as a European internal border under exit surveillance.

And a note on method: if the subject comes up in conversation, listen before you offer an opinion. Greek society's position on migration is genuinely ambivalent and does not map cleanly onto left and right; there is active solidarity and there is exhaustion, often in the same person. That ambivalence is the object of study, not an obstacle to reaching it.

Tempi, February 28, 2023, fifty-seven dead.

sections.heading: 2015: the year solidarity was the majority position
paragraphs: In 2015 close to a million people crossed into Greece, most of them Syrians fleeing a war in its fourth year, in inflatable boats from the Turkish coast to Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Kos, and Leros — crossings of between six and fifteen kilometers that cost hundreds of lives. It was the largest movement of people toward Europe since the Second World War.

Greek society's initial response was remarkable and deserves recording before what came after. On islands of a few thousand inhabitants, in a country at the worst moment of its own economic crisis, fishermen spent months on rescues, hotels housed people for free, schools turned into reception centers, and the so-called grandmothers of Lesbos — photographed bottle-feeding a baby just off the boats — became an international symbol. There were Nobel Peace Prize nominations for the islanders. All of that happened, largely, in the state's absence, since it was overwhelmed and in the midst of capital controls.

The observation that matters here is not a flattering one. It is that the spontaneous solidarity of 2015 was real and was not sustainable: it rested on the volunteer labor of small communities, with no resources and no relief, faced with a continuous flow. When the emergency became chronic, that base wore out, and something else filled the vacuum.

sections.heading: 2016: containment as European policy
paragraphs: In March 2016, the European Union and Turkey agreed on a statement under which Turkey would keep migrants on its territory and readmit those who arrived irregularly on the Greek islands, in exchange for billions of euros in financial assistance and commitments on visas and accession that were never fulfilled. The agreement sharply cut crossings and turned the eastern Aegean islands into containment zones: whoever arrived was held there until their case was resolved.

The result was Moria, on Lesbos: a camp designed for about three thousand people that came to hold more than twenty thousand, in conditions that reports from medical organizations and the United Nations repeatedly described as unacceptable. It burned down in September 2020. It was replaced by new facilities, funded by the European Union, defined as closed controlled-access centers: fenced perimeter, biometric entry and exit control, located far from urban centers. The official word is reception; the architecture is detention.

And there is the practice of pushbacks. Investigations by the Council of Europe, the European Ombudsman, human-rights organizations, and international media — including videos documenting the forced return of people already ashore back onto rafts adrift at sea — have maintained that the practice is systematic. An internal investigation by the European Anti-Fraud Office into the European border agency's knowledge and concealment of these practices led to the resignation of its director in 2022. The Greek government has always denied that the practice exists. The Pylos shipwreck, in June 2023, with more than five hundred missing and a timeline of the coast guard's actions that judicial and journalistic investigations contradict on substantial points, is the gravest episode of the period.

In 2024 the new European Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted, and its rollout is underway in 2026: accelerated border procedures, an expanded notion of safe third country, and flexible-solidarity mechanisms that let member states pay rather than take people in. Greece designated Turkey a safe third country for several nationalities, a decision Greek courts referred up to the Court of Justice of the European Union. The overall direction of European policy is externalization: making the filter happen before the border and outside its jurisdiction.

sections.heading: The border as an industry, and the labor it needs
paragraphs: Two sociological observations rarely appear together.

The first: border management is an economy. Camps, construction and security contractors, catering companies, surveillance technology, international staff, non-governmental organizations funded by European money. In islands with depressed economies, that spending generates employment and dependency, and produces actors with a material interest in the apparatus's continuation. The literature calls this the HUMANITARIAN BORDER: a regime that combines assistance and control, in which assistance is also the very thing that makes control tolerable and financeable.

The second, and more uncomfortable: the Greek economy needs the labor of these very people. Intensive agriculture in the Peloponnese and Crete, construction, domestic work, and much of seasonal hospitality depend on migrant labor, a significant share of it undocumented and therefore unable to make claims. The best-known case is Manolada, where in 2013 foremen shot at Bangladeshi workers demanding unpaid wages in the strawberry fields; the European Court of Human Rights found against Greece in 2017 for failing to prevent or adequately punish a situation of trafficking and forced labor. In 2025 the Greek government, under pressure from a shortage of farm workers, approved temporary regularization paths for migrants already present in the country: the same administration that toughens the border regularizes people when the productive sector demands it.

That contradiction is not individual hypocrisy: it is the structure of the matter. The European border regime does not stop workers from arriving, it REGULATES THE DEGREE OF VULNERABILITY they arrive with. Producing people without rights is what makes certain sectors competitive. Any serious analysis of migration has to start there, not in the moral debate about hospitality.

sections.heading: Peruvian mirror: the same curve in nine years
paragraphs: Since 2017, Peru has received more than a million and a half Venezuelans, the second-largest reception in the region after Colombia, in a country that at the time had neither a sized asylum system nor a consolidated migration policy.

The curve was the same as the Greek one, compressed. First, broad welcome, with the 2017 Temporary Stay Permit as one of the most generous responses in the region and a largely favorable social reception. Then, a hardening: the requirement of passport and humanitarian visa from 2018 and 2019, which pushed crossings toward informal routes. Then, a deterioration of public discourse, with media and political associations between migration and crime that the statistics do not support to the degree the debate suggests. And finally, the militarization of the Tumbes border in successive episodes between 2023 and 2025, with people trapped in no-man's-land between two states that did not want them.

And the same labor dependency: the service sector, street vending, delivery, restaurants, and construction absorbed that labor under conditions of informality, that is, with the same deliberate production of vulnerability.

And the same biographical irony as in Greece: more than three million Peruvians live abroad, and a large share of the country's families have someone who has migrated. As in the Greek case — a society made of the refugees of 1923 and the emigrants to Germany — the memory of one's own displacement produced no protection at all against the hardening that followed. That finding, repeated on two continents, forces us to abandon the idea that historical empathy operates politically. What operates is competition for scarce resources, the electoral use of fear, and the availability of a group that can be singled out.
